title: Applied anatomy: the hand — median and ulnar nerves, carpal tunnel

brief.scenario: This is a verbal applied anatomy viva on the wrist and palm. The examiner will describe structures by their position and relations, and ask you to name them and discuss their applied anatomy.
brief.task: Name each structure the examiner describes and answer the examiner's questions on the median and ulnar nerves in the hand.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Two nerves, two tunnels: median under the flexor retinaculum, ulnar over it in Guyon's canal.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Saying carpal tunnel syndrome numbs the thenar eminence. The palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the retinaculum.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Name the described structure, then give its attachments or course: "That is the flexor retinaculum. It attaches to..."

grid.label: Flexor retinaculum
grid.fail: Cannot name it from the description, or gives the wrong attachments.
grid.pass: Names it from the description: scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally, pisiform and hook of hamate medially.
grid.high: Adds that it bridges the carpal arch to roof the tunnel, with palmaris longus superficial to it.

grid.label: Contents of the carpal tunnel
grid.fail: Puts the ulnar nerve or artery in the tunnel.
grid.pass: Median nerve plus nine tendons: four of FDS, four of FDP, and flexor pollicis longus.
grid.high: Places the median nerve just deep to the retinaculum, anterior to the tendons; FPL in the radial bursa.

grid.label: Median nerve in the hand
grid.fail: Says carpal tunnel compression numbs the thenar skin, or omits the recurrent motor branch.
grid.pass: Recurrent branch to abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis; sensation to the palmar lateral three and a half digits.
grid.high: Adds the lateral two lumbricals, and explains why thenar skin is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

grid.label: Ulnar nerve at the wrist
grid.fail: Places the ulnar nerve inside the carpal tunnel.
grid.pass: Superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal, between pisiform and hook of hamate, with the ulnar artery.
grid.high: Deep branch: hypothenar muscles, interossei, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis. Superficial branch: medial one and a half digits.

grid.label: Clinical signs
grid.fail: Cannot name a test for either nerve.
grid.borderline: Names Tinel's and Phalen's tests but cannot say what a positive result shows.
grid.pass: Tinel's and Phalen's for median compression, Froment's sign for ulnar weakness, and what a positive result shows.
grid.high: Explains the ulnar paradox: an elbow lesion claws less than a wrist lesion, because FDP to the ring and little fingers is also lost.

grid.label: Carpal tunnel release
grid.fail: Cannot say what is at risk.
grid.pass: Divides the flexor retinaculum, protecting the recurrent motor branch and the palmar cutaneous branch.
grid.high: Incision in line with the radial border of the ring finger, ulnar to the thenar crease; superficial palmar arch just distal.

grid.label: Root values and cords
grid.fail: Gives root values for the wrong nerve.
grid.pass: Median C6–T1, sometimes C5; ulnar C8–T1, sometimes C7.
grid.high: Adds cords: median from the lateral and medial cords, ulnar from the medial cord.

grid.label: Handling uncertainty
grid.fail: Names a structure confidently and wrongly when unsure.
grid.pass: States uncertainty, then reasons from the described position and course before naming.
grid.high: Gives a two-item differential with a reason, then commits.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A thick transverse fibrous band spans the front of the carpal bones at the base of the palm, attached at each side to bony prominences of the carpus. What is it?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The median nerve, the ulnar nerve and the flexor tendons.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A patient with carpal tunnel syndrome says her thenar eminence is numb. Is that expected?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, the median nerve supplies that skin.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Where is the ulnar nerve at the wrist?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: In the carpal tunnel, next to the median nerve.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A short branch leaves the lateral side of the nerve at the distal edge of that band and turns back proximally into the thenar eminence. What is it?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's definitely the palmar cutaneous branch.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A thick transverse fibrous band spans the front of the carpal bones at the base of the palm, attached at each side to bony prominences of the carpus. What is it, and where exactly does it attach?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That is the flexor retinaculum. It attaches to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally, and the pisiform and hook of hamate medially.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of profundus, and flexor pollicis longus.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What does the median nerve supply in the hand?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Through the recurrent branch, abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis. It gives sensation to the palmar lateral three and a half digits.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It runs superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal, between the pisiform and the hook of hamate, with the ulnar artery.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you test for median compression, and for ulnar weakness?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Tinel's, tapping over the tunnel, and Phalen's, holding the wrist flexed, both reproduce tingling in the median territory. Froment's sign shows weak adductor pollicis: the thumb flexes at the IP joint to grip paper.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Median C6 to T1, sometimes C5. Ulnar C8 and T1, sometimes C7.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: In a carpal tunnel release, what are you protecting?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The recurrent motor branch and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A short branch leaves the lateral side of the nerve at the distal edge of that band and turns back proximally into the thenar eminence. What is it?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm not certain. A branch that leaves the median nerve as it emerges from the tunnel and turns back into the thenar eminence is heading for the thenar muscles, so I think it's the recurrent motor branch.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: A thick transverse fibrous band spans the front of the carpal bones at the base of the palm, attached at each side to bony prominences of the carpus. What is it, and where exactly does it attach?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is the flexor retinaculum: scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally, pisiform and hook of hamate medially. It roofs the carpal arch, and palmaris longus lies superficial to it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The median nerve and nine tendons. The nerve lies just deep to the retinaculum, in front of the tendons, which is why it is the structure compressed. Flexor pollicis longus sits in the radial bursa.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: A patient with carpal tunnel syndrome has numb fingers but normal sensation over the thenar eminence. Why?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve above the wrist and passes superficial to the retinaculum, so thenar skin is spared. The recurrent branch supplies the thenar muscles, and digital branches the lateral two lumbricals.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It passes over the retinaculum in Guyon's canal. The deep branch supplies the hypothenar muscles, interossei, medial two lumbricals and adductor pollicis; the superficial branch supplies the medial one and a half digits.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why can a high ulnar lesion look less dramatic?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's the ulnar paradox. At the elbow, FDP to the ring and little fingers is lost too, so there is less clawing than with a wrist lesion, where FDP still flexes those fingers.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Median C6 to T1, sometimes C5, from the lateral and medial cords. Ulnar C8 and T1, sometimes C7, from the medial cord.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Where would you make the incision for a release?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In line with the radial border of the ring finger, ulnar to the thenar crease. That protects the recurrent motor and palmar cutaneous branches, and I'd stop short of the superficial palmar arch distally.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: A short branch leaves the lateral side of the nerve at the distal edge of that band and turns back proximally into the thenar eminence. What is it?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's either the recurrent motor branch or a palmar digital branch to the thumb. A digital branch runs on distally; this one turns back proximally into the thenar muscles from the distal edge of the retinaculum, so it's the recurrent motor branch.

failures.move: Naming Tinel's and Phalen's without saying what a positive test shows.
failures.consequence: Shows the test's name, not the understanding the question is testing.

failures.move: Not knowing what is at risk in a carpal tunnel release.
failures.consequence: Misses the surgical point of the station: the recurrent motor branch can be cut.

failures.move: Mixing up median and ulnar root values.
failures.consequence: Undermines every later answer about where a lesion lies.

failures.move: Saying carpal tunnel syndrome numbs the thenar eminence.
failures.consequence: Misses the palmar cutaneous branch, the detail that separates a wrist lesion from a proximal one.

recovery.line: I can't identify that with certainty. From its position and course, I'd favour X over Y, because…
The ulnar nerve comes from the medial cord, so it carries C8 and T1.

knowledge.fact: Flexor retinaculum: scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally; pisiform and hook of hamate medially.
Carpal tunnel contents: median nerve plus nine tendons (FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL).
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the retinaculum, so thenar skin is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Guyon's canal: ulnar nerve and artery, between pisiform and hook of hamate.
Froment's sign: thumb IP flexion (FPL, median) compensates for weak adductor pollicis (ulnar).

NICE CKS (August 2026): refer if the diagnosis is unclear, symptoms persist despite a trial of conservative treatment (night splint or a single steroid injection, with review at 6 weeks), symptoms are progressive or severe, or symptoms recur after surgery.

recall.think: Which tunnel, which nerve, and which branch is spared?
recall.say: "Median under the retinaculum; ulnar over it, in Guyon's canal."

recall.finish: Release in line with the radial border of the ring finger; protect the recurrent motor branch.

partner.opening: This is a verbal viva on the wrist and palm. I'll describe structures by their position; name each one, then we'll discuss its applied anatomy.

reveals.finding: Read out: a thick transverse fibrous band spans the front of the carpal bones at the base of the palm, attached at each side to bony prominences of the carpus. Ask what it is and where it attaches.
Read out: deep to this band is a tunnel. A flattened nerve lies immediately beneath the band, with a group of long flexor tendons behind it. Ask what passes through the tunnel.
Read out: a short branch leaves the lateral side of that nerve at the distal edge of the band and turns back proximally into the thenar eminence. Ask what it is.
Read out: a nerve and an artery run superficial to the band on its medial side, just lateral to the pisiform. Ask where they lie and what the nerve is.

push.question: What does the median nerve supply in the hand?
push.expect: Recurrent branch: APB, opponens, FPB. Sensation: palmar lateral 3½ digits. Lateral two lumbricals.

push.question: How would you test for median compression and for ulnar weakness?
push.expect: Tinel's, Phalen's, Froment's sign, and what each positive result shows.

push.question: What are the root values?
push.expect: Median C6–T1 (sometimes C5); ulnar C8–T1 (sometimes C7).

push.question: What do you protect in a carpal tunnel release?
push.expect: Recurrent motor and palmar cutaneous branches; incision in line with the radial border of the ring finger.

curveballs.prompt: Her thenar skin is numb too. Is this still carpal tunnel syndrome?
curveballs.safeAnswer: It suggests a more proximal median lesion, because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum.

curveballs.prompt: Why is clawing worse with a wrist lesion than an elbow lesion?
curveballs.safeAnswer: The ulnar paradox: an elbow lesion also paralyses FDP to the ring and little fingers.

curveballs.prompt: Which muscle does Froment's sign test?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Adductor pollicis (ulnar); flexor pollicis longus (median) substitutes.
